title: Creation Hub — an AI agent workspace for campaign personalization
description: I architected and shipped Creation Hub, the AI-assisted workspace inside Optimeleon's dashboard where marketers generate landing-page hypotheses, variants, and audience segments by talking to an agent. I designed the command-driven protocol that turns a streaming LLM into 16 interactive UI cards, and led the feature from first commit through six months of team delivery.

sections.title: A chat box is a terrible place to make a decision

items.src: Optimeleon personalizes landing pages: you write a hypothesis about a slice of your traffic, build a page variant for it, and measure whether it converts better than the baseline. The bottleneck was never the measuring. It was everything before it — a marketer staring at a blank hypothesis form with no idea what to write.

We had an AI agent service that could actually do the thinking: read a customer's Meta or Google ads, extract the core marketing concepts from their site, identify which visitor segments were underperforming. What we didn't have was a way for a marketer to use any of it. The output of an LLM is text, and text is where a workflow goes to die.

If the agent proposed six hypotheses, the user had to copy them, one at a time, into a form on another page. If it surfaced a winning variant, they had to go find it themselves. If it suggested an audience segment with eight filter conditions, they had to rebuild it by hand. The intelligence was real and the friction ate all of it.

src: Four distinct AI capabilities existed on the backend with no coherent front door.
Every agent output was prose — nothing was clickable, saveable, or connected to the objects it described.
The agent leaked internal UUIDs into its answers, so users saw raw variant IDs instead of names.
Nothing the agent produced could be acted on without leaving the conversation.

sections.title: Treat the model's output as a UI protocol, not a transcript

items.src: Core Decision
The agent doesn't send text. It sends commands.

The decision the whole feature rests on: the socket carries two different kinds of message. Prose streams token-by-token over a `chat_response` event and renders as markdown. But when the agent wants the user to *do* something, it emits a `command` event instead — a named string plus a payload — and the client renders a real, interactive React component in the message stream. A hypothesis list becomes a multi-select table with a save button. A set of ads becomes a picker. A proposed segment becomes an editable filter builder that writes straight to the database.

That single indirection is what lets a conversation end in a saved database row instead of a paragraph the user has to retype. It also meant the agent team could ship a new capability without me touching the transport: they emit a new command name, I register a component against it.

src.title: One transport, four agents
src.desc: Ad-to-Variant, Core Concepts, Clone-From-Winner and Segment Analysis are four completely different guided flows, but they share one socket, one streaming state machine, and one card registry. Each agent is a different conversation over identical plumbing.

src.title: A normalization layer between model and props
src.desc: The AI's payloads are heterogeneous and snake_cased, and their shape changed as the agent team iterated. A single transformer module absorbs that churn and emits stable component props — so a schema change on their side is a diff in one file, not fifteen components.

src.title: Chat history is deliberately ephemeral
src.desc: Conversations live in memory and are discarded when the panel closes. Persisting them meant reconciling stored history against socket resume and stale variant IDs — real complexity for a flow whose whole purpose is to terminate in a saved hypothesis. The saved artifact is the memory.

src.title: Every card gets its own error boundary
src.desc: The agent is a language model, so a malformed payload isn't an edge case — it's Tuesday. Each rendered card is isolated, so one bad response degrades to a single failed card instead of blanking the entire conversation.

items.src: Engineering Hurdle 01
Streaming tokens have no obligation to arrive in order

The agent's response lifecycle is a three-beat protocol — `start`, then a run of `stream` tokens, then `end` — and the naive implementation assumes they arrive in that order. They don't always. A `stream` token can land before its `start`, and the message it belongs to doesn't exist yet. I built the append path to create the message lazily when that happens, tracking the in-flight message by index in a ref so concatenation never races React's batched state updates.

src: FIX: A ref-tracked stream index plus lazy message creation on out-of-order tokens
RESULT: Streaming survives token reordering without dropping or duplicating text

items.src: Engineering Hurdle 02
The model kept leaking raw UUIDs into its prose

The segment agent reasons over variant performance, so it holds variant UUIDs — and it would drop them straight into sentences. Users would read "variant 3f9a2c1e-… outperformed the baseline" and have no idea which page that was. Worse, the model sometimes inserted stray whitespace mid-UUID while streaming, so a naive match missed it entirely. I resolve every variant for the session into a lookup map up front, then rewrite the streamed markdown with a whitespace-tolerant UUID pattern, substituting human variant names before the text ever renders.

src: FIX: Session-scoped variant map plus whitespace-tolerant UUID substitution over streamed markdown
RESULT: Users read variant names, not internal identifiers, even when the model formats badly

items.src: Engineering Hurdle 03
Buttons in a chat have to speak the agent's language

When a user selects three hypotheses and clicks generate, the agent needs to know — but it's a language model mid-conversation, not a state machine with an RPC surface. Structured actions exist for session lifecycle, but mid-flow branching had to re-enter the model's own context. So a click emits a synthetic user turn back over the socket: the UI speaks to the agent in the only interface it truly has. It's an unusual shape, and it's the honest one — the LLM's natural-language interface *is* the API.

src: FIX: Card actions emit synthetic user turns, so the model's own context drives the next step
RESULT: Multi-turn guided flows branch on button clicks without a parallel state machine to keep in sync

items.src: Engineering Hurdle 04
Six months of other people's features landing on my foundation

I opened Creation Hub; seven other engineers then shipped into it — segment editing, winning-variant cloning, campaign reports, Google keyword-level ad matching. The architecture had to hold up under contributors who had never read it. The command registry did that work: it made the extension point so obvious that new capabilities landed as a new entry and a new component, without anyone needing to touch the socket lifecycle or the streaming reducer.

src: FIX: A single frozen registry as the one documented extension point
RESULT: 72 commits from 8 contributors, with the transport layer effectively untouched after the initial build

src.label: AI commands mapped to interactive UI cards
Guided agent flows on one shared transport
Lines across 51 files, shipped over 6 months

items.src: Every number here is counted from the repository at the close of the period — the command registry, the agent flows, and the module's own line and file count. They measure the shape and reach of what shipped, not its business outcome; adoption and conversion figures live in the product's own analytics and are deliberately not claimed here.

Rewrites of the socket layer after the initial build

items.src: An AI feature is only as good as the thing the user can click at the end of it. The model was never the hard part — the hard part was refusing to let its output stay as text.

The instinct when you wire up an LLM is to render what it says. The better move is to make it say things that render into something actionable — and then design the contract that makes that cheap. The command registry took an afternoon to design and it is the reason seven engineers could extend this feature for six months without anyone touching the transport.

The other lesson was about where to spend defensive effort. Models produce malformed output; that isn't an exception path, it's the steady state. Error boundaries per card, tolerance for out-of-order tokens, and regexes that expect the model to format badly weren't paranoia. They were the difference between a demo and something a customer uses on a Monday morning.
